extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literary criticism, translators, and creative writers studying Aristotle's Poetics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative principles for composing and judging poetic fiction (epic, tragedy, romance), covering plausibility, diction, unity, use of the marvellous, metre, and responses to criticism as set out in Aristotle's Poetics with editorial commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: The marvellous is appetizing (use of wonder)
rubrics_metrics.description: Marvelling produces desire and pleasure; the marvellous (what excites wonder) is appetizing and can be used to engage the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce marvellous elements to stimulate the audience's desire to 'make out' the situation; the recounter often adds picturesque detail to increase this effect (example: Euryclea shedding tears). Use wonder to restore the audience's natural condition, producing pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use picturesque details to lend plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: When inventing or reporting something not witnessed, add small concrete details (picturesque detail) that give the account plausibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Append attendant facts that would naturally accompany the fiction (the mind assumes A accompanies B); these plausible attendant details make a fiction seem true (example: adding actions that typically accompany crying).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer a plausible impossibility to an unconvincing possibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrative that contains an impossible element is preferable if that impossibility is nonetheless plausible to the audience, rather than a possible event that is unconvincing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for subjective plausibility: if the audience can be led to accept an impossibility (by preparation/detail), it is better than an inadequately motivated 'realistic' event that fails to convince.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep unnatural elements in the background or fully prepare them
rubrics_metrics.description: If the story requires elements that violate ordinary causation (the unnatural), they should generally be kept in the background; if made central, they must be emphasized and thoroughly prepared for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The unnatural as a conspicuous foreground element risks absurdity (unless the poet prepares the hearer thoroughly). Rotteken's advice: either conceal the unnatural or prepare the audience fully by emphasis and groundwork.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take account of audience condition and media (subjectivity and music/metre)
rubrics_metrics.description: The acceptability of violations of possibility depends on subjective factors: metre, music, and other formal elements can lull critical power and render the marvellous acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use metric, musical, or performative devices to prepare or condition the audience (e.g., metre/music can make a ghost less surprising). Consider the audience's predisposition (creepiness, cultural expectations) when introducing extraordinary elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not make the story depend on unaccountable features unless necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: A story should not require unaccountable or gratuitous features from the outset; if such features are introduced, there should be no obvious, more intelligible alternative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid plots that only work because of inexplicable contrivances. If an unaccountable element is used, justify it so that no obvious better procedure is apparent (example: certain Odyssey episodes work only because of Homer's skill).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid glaring anachronism; judge by audience familiarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Anachronisms should be avoided if they are glaring and detectable by the audience; if not glaring, they may be unobjectionable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the item (institution, object, word) would be detected as anachronistic by contemporary listeners/readers; minor or non-glaring anachronisms may be tolerated (example: Pythian Games in Sophocles' Electra).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction must suit the character and occasion; avoid over-brilliance in 'flat' passages
rubrics_metrics.description: Care with diction is essential, especially in 'flat' passages (those without psychology or reasoning); over-brilliant wording can obscure psychology and argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accommodate diction to the character (grandiloquence unsuited to humble characters). Employ the smallest exertion (economical means) appropriate to effect; do not use dazzling language where clarity of feeling or reasoning is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economical employment of means (least exertion principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the minimal necessary means to achieve the poetic effect; excessive display can undermine clarity or believability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor restraint: let metre, diction, and imagery do only what's needed. Over-elaboration can distract; this principle underlies aesthetic economy and supports clarity of portrayal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish poetical correctness from scientific or factual correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Correctness in poetry is not identical with correctness in other sciences (e.g., medicine); poetic errors may be tolerated if they serve poetic ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two kinds of poetical incorrectness: direct (inability to portray a theme as chosen) and indirect (wrong choice e.g., portraying a horse unnaturally). If adherence to scientific truth would not interfere with poetic ends, avoid the error; otherwise poetic effect may warrant deviation (example: poets defending Homeric practices as traditional).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three modes of portrayal: the real, the conventional (traditional), or the ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet's characters must portray either the real (actual), the conventional/traditional, or the ideal; each mode justifies different poetic choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If criticized as 'untrue,' reply by arguing that characters are idealized (type), represent tradition, or are realistic portrayals of their time. Choose portrayal mode consciously and defend choices accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge utterance/performance in relation to subject, object, occasion, beneficiary and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriateness of speech or action depends on context: the subject matter, the audience, the occasion, who benefits, and the purpose served.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assess lines or actions in isolation; evaluate them by their function within the situation (what advantage or detriment they secure). Contextual appropriateness can justify otherwise objectionable material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five principal critical objections (classification of faults)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical objections fall into five categories: impossible, unnatural, immoral, inconsistent, or inartistic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or defending a passage, identify which of these five charges is being made; the correct line of rebuttal depends on the category (see the twelve solutions for responses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Twelve dialectical/interpretive solutions to apparent faults
rubrics_metrics.description: There are multiple ways to defend or explain passages that seem faulty: (in summary) realistic defense, conventional/traditional defense, idealistic defense, conflict-with-science defense, incidental/accidental error, foreign/loan word, metaphorical usage, familiar usage, mistaken sense (different grammatical/lexical parsing), wrong intonation, distinguishing senses, and wrong application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these interpretive tactics when a passage seems inconsistent or incorrect: propose alternative intonation or parsing; show that a word is used by transference (species/genus); read as dialectal or metaphorical; argue the passage is traditional; claim idealization; or show the error is incidental rather than essential. The commentary gives examples (e.g., 'all' as genus-for-species transference; 'raw' reinterpreted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve apparent verbal or grammatical inconsistencies by close linguistic methods
rubrics_metrics.description: When a phrase appears inconsistent, examine how many senses the key words could bear, consider grammatical alternatives, intonation, and dialectal usages to arrive at a natural reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tools from dialectic/sophistic analysis: change of intonation, distinguishing senses, noting grammatical ambiguity (e.g., comparative vs genitive readings), and familiar or transferred usages. These linguistic devices can reconcile apparent contradictions without blaming the poet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid gratuitous 'unnatural' moral or depraved insertions
rubrics_metrics.description: Material is rightly censured as 'unnatural' or 'immoral' when introduced without necessity or appropriate grounds (e.g., depravity added gratuitously to a character).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure moral elements serve dramatic or poetic purpose; gratuitous departures into depravity or unethical portrayal are legitimate grounds for censure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre/form selection judged by audience and realization of artistic purpose (Epic vs Tragedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose form (epic, tragedy, romance) with regard to its audience, unity, compression, and ability to realize its artistic purpose; tragedy may be superior if it realizes purpose more fully (unity, focused effect, music/exhibition) whereas epic addresses a refined readership and may be diffuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess: audience sophistication (refined vs popular), whether pantomimic or gestural elements are necessary, unity of plot (romance often less unified), compression (shorter, concentrated works may give more pleasure), and the advantages of performance (music/exhibition). Consider whether a form's strengths align with the intended artistic ends.
